shots.narration:
Rei knew the notebook belonged to him before he recognised anything inside it.

There was a pressure to the handwriting, the same habit of bearing down at the end of a line. He still did it when he was tired. He passed a finger beside the letters without touching them.

A timetable. Instructions divided into intervals.

He remembered counting those intervals. That much came without effort. When he tried to follow the memory farther, there was no room around it, no continuous sequence he could walk through. He looked up at his own table and waited until the present settled around him again.

Yuriko had left the book with him years ago. It had not arrived today with a message he had failed to understand. Nothing about the paper had changed because he had finally opened it.

He brought out a drawing made after they had escaped and placed it beside the timetable.

shots.narration:
The difference between the pages bothered him. He had expected to be able to recognise himself more easily in one than the other. Instead he recognised the pressure of his hand in both.

“I made this too,” he said.

The words sounded oddly formal in the empty room. He looked at the drawing again.

No one had assigned it to him. He had chosen where the first line went.

He wrote down what he could actually read and what he remembered of counting. When he reached the point where the memory stopped, he stopped writing. The empty space looked deliberate now. He left it there.

The old seal matched the name on a present-day Kurose House notice. A name surviving did not tell him who had survived with it, or whether anyone had. He wanted records he could check without asking his memory to manufacture the missing years.

shots.narration:
Yuriko stopped when she saw the notebook.

“You found it.”

“I knew where it was.” Rei looked down. “I opened it.”

She nodded, accepting the difference. For a moment he wished she would say something ordinary enough to make him stop waiting for her reaction.

“Do you want me to sit?” she asked.

He moved a chair away from the table with his foot.

“I recognised the writing,” he said. “Then I couldn't tell whether I remembered what it said or just remembered being told things like it.”

shots.narration:
Yuriko leaned forward only far enough to see the part he turned toward her.

“I don't want to answer that for you.”

“You were there.”

“Not everywhere you were.”

He looked at her. She was holding herself carefully, as though trying not to take up space he had not offered.

“I know,” he said. “Sorry.”

“You can ask me. I just need to be allowed to say I don't know.”

shots.narration:
Rei glanced at the other drawing. “I keep thinking I should be able to look at a page.”

“You are looking at it.”

“Without doing this.”

“Doing what?”

He couldn't find a description that didn't sound smaller than it felt.

Yuriko waited. Then she said, “Would you like me to put the other things away? Or leave them?”

“Leave them.”

FLASHBACK — Golden Dragon, early months

Rei had come in alone after a shoot. He wanted food and a place where no one was asking him to hold a position. His sketchbook rested against his leg beneath the table.

“Give me that one. I’ll replace it.”

“It’s all right.”

FLASHBACK — Later visits, after their first meeting

Garrett remembered his order the next time. Rei told himself that was a good reason to return again. The food was good. It was on his way often enough. He could sit without being hurried.

On a later evening, Garrett asked about the sketchbook and actually waited while Rei explained what he was trying to make.

Another night, Rei stayed while the bowls were washed.

“You don't have to do that,” Garrett said when Rei picked up a cloth.

“I know.”

Garrett looked at him, then slid a bowl within reach.

shots.narration:
PRESENT DAY

Rei became aware of the room by degrees: the chair under him, the light across his table, the page he had been holding too tightly.

He put it down before the corner tore.

For a moment he wanted to apologise to it. The thought made him close his eyes. It was paper. He could take care of it, but taking care of it could not change that morning.

He sat until he could look at the drawing without trying to force himself back into the courtyard. Later, if Sophie was available and he chose company, he would meet her somewhere they could walk. He did not need to make that arrangement before he had finished breathing through this moment.

“Do you have somewhere in mind?” Sophie asked.

“No.”

“Good. I was going to pretend I did.”

Rei looked at her. She lifted one shoulder, and he felt the first small release of tension since leaving home.

shots.narration:
Back home, Rei opened to the miniature city again.

There was a temptation to make the page carry a conclusion: something he had learned, something he could finally promise. He could not find a sentence that did not ask too much of a drawing two boys had made during lunch.

He began with the crooked roof. Then the argument about the street. He wrote that Marcus had made him laugh and sometimes made him impatient. When he reached Joseph's bullying, he recorded what he knew without making it the only thing on the page. He did not invent the words Marcus had never had a chance to say to him.

The gaps in his childhood memory and the grief he remembered from school were different things. He did not need to make either explain the other. He closed his notes when he had written what he could honestly say.

shots.narration:
“The reference identifies the archive copy.”

He looked back at the page. “This doesn't tell me what happens if someone changes their mind.”

“I can give you the public form. I can't answer for records I don't have.”

The restraint in the answer irritated him before he recognised that it was reasonable. He had no basis to decide what Robin knew about the programme beyond the material being supplied.

“Right,” he said. “Thank you.”

He nearly added another question that was really an accusation. Instead he compared the project number and noted the source.

Outside, he stood with the form held flat between his hands. The referral and the contract shared a reference. That warranted another question. It did not turn the person at the desk into an accomplice or put him any closer to knowing what Joseph would admit.

shots.narration:
The complaint was anonymised. Rei read it without trying to supply a face.

People had attempted to withdraw. The records described restraint trials. The authorisation bore Joseph's name.

He went back to the dates, the project number, the connection to the contract. He needed the connection to hold without his anger holding it together.

It did.

For a while he could hear nothing in the room except paper moving beneath his hands. He thought of the participation form, its careful headings, the space where a person could have believed they were being asked.

“They said they wanted to stop,” he said quietly.

This time the sentence belonged to the documents in front of him. He did not need a school memory to make the conduct wrong.

He kept the authorisation with the complaint and left the unanswered questions visible. The equipment records identified the compound and offices. He copied what he would need before approaching headquarters.

shots.narration:
Outside, Rei stopped before choosing a direction.

He could still hear the name in Daichi's voice. A present-day voice. He had spent much of the meeting making sure he did not confuse that with another one.

The records mattered. He had asked for evidence and received it. He could not decide that evidence only counted when it made the choice easier.

But the documents did not have to live with the sound of the name afterward. He did.

If he led, he would be responsible for people whose lives were not an extension of his past. If he left, he would have to let the organisation continue without making its future his task. If he dismantled it, he would be acting against the successor that existed now, not reaching backward to the original clan.

He stood until those were three separate thoughts.

“I don't have to answer in that room,” he said.

shots.narration:
Garrett listened until Rei had finished the part he was willing to tell.

“You could be more helpful.”

“And I am not telling you how to feel about that.”

Daichi's expression stayed measured. “You have given us an answer.”

Rei looked once more at the room. It would continue to exist when he left. There were people here who would have tomorrow's concerns without him being responsible for all of them.

It was a small freedom, too ordinary to announce. He stood with it for a while before walking on.

shots.narration:
The operations had closed. The staff survived and left their organisational duties. Rei recorded the outcome in plain language, then read it again.

He had wanted to know what would remain in him after the name no longer belonged to a functioning organisation he could approach. The answer did not arrive with the final victory.

He could still remember the timetable. The gaps were still gaps.

He sat until he could separate exhaustion from whatever else he was feeling. There would be time to describe it more accurately. For now he would not call the closure a restored childhood, or ask the people who had left to agree that it was.

“Do you want us to ask you not to go?” Emily said.

Rei looked at her. “I don't know.”

“I don't know whether it would help either.” She rubbed her hands together. “I don't want to say something brave just because you're about to leave.”

Sophie leaned forward. “What can you actually tell us?”

“That I'm going alone. That I don't know how long it'll take.”

“Then don't give us a time you made up,” Sophie said.

He nodded.

“And if I don't?”

“Then we can have a very serious argument about dumplings.”

The practical answer was easier to carry than a promise of safety. He left the conversation knowing there was somewhere he could arrive without having to begin with a successful ending.

Joseph's sleeves parted around the reinforced arms. Rei heard the mechanism before the powered frame locked into place.

“Awakened people have advantages the rest of us never chose,” Joseph said. “I built mine.”

“And everyone in those records was supposed to pay for it?”

Joseph's expression hardened. “This is bigger than your old grievances.”

There it was: the invitation to become a boy in a courtyard again, furious enough to lose the sentence he had come to say.

Rei held the papers still.

shots.narration:
“You don't get to make what you're doing now disappear by calling me angry.”

“You are angry.”

“Yes.”

The admission seemed to leave Joseph with less to interrupt.

“You hurt Marcus,” Rei said. “You made him afraid of rooms he had to walk into. And then you talked about it as if it was something too small to answer for.”

“That was school.”

shots.narration:
The powered frame failed. The fight was over. Rei listened to the machinery falling silent.

Joseph spoke before Rei had decided what he wanted to say.

“I bullied Marcus. I chose to hurt him, and then pretended it didn't matter.”

Rei stood still.

“I am sorry,” Joseph said. “I am sorry for what I did to these people too.”

For years, Rei had imagined making him acknowledge it. He had never imagined the silence immediately afterward with any accuracy.

Marcus did not come into the room. The film remained unfinished. There were still people in this programme who needed the outcome to mean more than a conversation between two former classmates.

“The programme is stopped,” he said. Sophie nodded once. “All right.” She did not ask him to make that mean everything was finished.

He looked at the glass.

“I don't know what to say about it.”

“You already asked for water. That was useful.”

He gave a tired breath that almost became a laugh.

“I thought I'd be better at coming back.”

“There's no performance requirement.”

shots.narration:
Rei put the old timetable and the current records on different parts of the table.

The distinction had become easier to describe. It had not become effortless to feel.

Tomorrow there would be questions from people whose present lives he had agreed to help govern. He would answer them as honestly as he could. The title did not entitle him to call uncertainty weakness in someone else.

The Blackstone programme was stopped. Joseph had acknowledged what he had done. Rei kept the acknowledgement in its actual place: something that had happened, not a replacement for what had happened before it.

He opened the storyboard once more. The pigeon was still on the page.

“I'm keeping this,” he said.

There was no one there who needed convincing. He could put it away and return to it another day. He could draw something else without asking whether that meant he had forgotten.

shots.narration:
“Do you want me to ask you not to go?” Emily asked.

“I don’t know.”

“I don’t know whether it would help either. I don’t want to say something brave just because you’re about to leave.”

Rei looked at her hands, then back at her face. “I’m going alone. I don’t know how long it will take.”

“Then don’t promise me a time. I’d like to see you afterward. Not for a report.”

“I might not be good company.”

“You can let me decide whether I want the company.”

He smiled a little. “I can tell you when I’m able.”

“That would help.” She paused. “Please be careful.”

“I’ll pay attention,” he said. It was the promise he could make.

“What can you actually tell me?” Sophie asked.

“That I’m going alone. That I don’t know how long it will take.”
